title: Unit 3: Differentiation: Composite, Implicit, and Inverse Functions

topics.name: The chain rule
covers: The chain rule for differentiating composite functions

topics.name: Inverse functions and higher-order derivatives
covers: Differentiation of general and particular inverse functions

guide.title: Chain rule, implicit and inverse derivatives: review guide
guide.intro: This unit extends derivatives to functions inside other functions, to curves not written as y = f(x), and to inverse functions.

sections.title: The chain rule
body: For a composite function, differentiate the outside function (keeping the inside the same), then multiply by the derivative of the inside.
points: Spot the inside: in (3x + 1)⁵ it is 3x + 1. In e^(x²) it is x². In ln(x² + 1) it is x² + 1.
With a table of values, evaluate the outer derivative at g(a), not at a.

sections.title: Implicit differentiation
body: Differentiate both sides with respect to x. Every time you differentiate an expression in y, multiply by dy/dx, because y depends on x. Then solve for dy/dx.
points: d/dx (xy) needs the product rule: y + x · dy/dx.

sections.title: Inverse functions and higher derivatives
body: If g is the inverse of f and f(a) = b, then g′(b) = 1/f′(a). Find a first by solving f(a) = b. Do not evaluate f′ at b.
points: The second derivative f″ is the derivative of f′. It measures how the slope changes.

example.prompt: Find dy/dx for x² + y² = 25 at the point (3, 4).
example.solution: Differentiate: 2x + 2y · dy/dx = 0, so dy/dx = −x/y. At (3, 4), dy/dx = −3/4.

misconceptions: “The chain rule is only for powers.”
Any function inside another one needs it: e^(x²), sin(5x), ln(x² + 1).
Because y depends on x, it is 2y · dy/dx.
Use 1/f′(a), where f(a) = b. Evaluate f′ at the matching input of f.

questions.explanation: The derivative of e^u is e^u · u′. With u = x², u′ = 2x, so the derivative is 2x · e^(x²).
choiceExplanations: The exponent stays x². Only the outside factor 2x comes from the inside derivative.
e^x is its own derivative, but here the exponent is x², so the chain rule adds a factor of 2x.
This uses the power rule on the exponent. The variable is in the exponent, so use the exponential rule.

questions.prompt: f(x) = x³ + x and g is the inverse of f. What is g′(2)?
questions.explanation: Solve f(a) = 2: a³ + a = 2 gives a = 1. Then f′(x) = 3x² + 1, so f′(1) = 4 and g′(2) = 1/f′(1) = 1/4.
choiceExplanations: This forgets to take the reciprocal: g′(2) = 1/f′(1).
This evaluates f′ at 2 and forgets the reciprocal.
This evaluates f′ at 2 (f′(2) = 13). Use the input a where f(a) = 2, which is a = 1.
questions.licenseOrRights: Original question written for StudySprint. The linked College Board page was only used to confirm the unit's title and scope.

questions.explanation: d/dx ln u = u′/u. With u = x² + 1 and u′ = 2x, the derivative is 2x/(x² + 1).
choiceExplanations: This divides 1 by the inside derivative. The rule is the inside derivative divided by the inside: 2x/(x² + 1).
This forgets the chain rule factor u′ = 2x.
There is no product here. ln is applied to x² + 1, so use the chain rule.

questions.prompt: xy + y² = 6. What is dy/dx at the point (1, 2)?
questions.explanation: Differentiate: y + x · dy/dx + 2y · dy/dx = 0. So dy/dx = −y/(x + 2y). At (1, 2): −2/(1 + 4) = −2/5.
choiceExplanations: 0 results from writing d/dx(xy) as just x · dy/dx. The product rule also gives a y term.
−6 results from writing d/dx(y²) as 2y without the factor dy/dx.
−1/2 results from writing d/dx(xy) as just y and dropping x · dy/dx.
